title: What are the National Registry recertification requirements for EMTs and paramedics?
description: National Registry EMS recertification as at November 2026: two year cycle, NCCP credits by level, the 2025 model, skills verification and audit records.
shortAnswer: The National Registry of Emergency Medical Technicians (National Registry) requires nationally certified EMS clinicians to recertify every two years, either by passing the cognitive examination or by completing continuing education under the National Continued Competency Program (NCCP). The NCCP requires 16 credits for Emergency Medical Responders, 40 for EMTs, 50 for Advanced EMTs and 60 for Paramedics, split 50% national, 25% local or state and 25% individual. Active status also needs agency affiliation and verified skills.
keyTakeaways: Certification lasts two years; after an approved recertification the new expiration date is two years after the current one.
NCCP credit totals are 16 (EMR), 40 (EMT), 50 (AEMT) and 60 (Paramedic), with the national component at 50% and local or state and individual components at 25% each.
The 2025 NCCP model applies from April 1, 2025 for EMTs, AEMTs and Paramedics, and from October 1, 2025 for EMRs.
EMT, AEMT and Paramedic certifications expire on March 31; education must be complete by then, with a $50 late or reinstatement window to April 30.
Clinicians must keep recertification documentation for at least three years because the National Registry runs random audits.
jurisdiction: United States (national EMS certification; state EMS offices license practice)
regulator: National Registry of Emergency Medical Technicians (National Registry); state EMS offices, such as the Wisconsin Department of Health Services, license EMS clinicians
appliesTo: Nationally certified Emergency Medical Responders (NREMR), EMTs (NREMT), Advanced EMTs (NRAEMT) and Paramedics (NRP)
EMS agencies, fire departments and hospital based services whose training officers and medical directors verify skills
EMS education programs and CAPCE accredited continuing education providers
State EMS offices that accept National Registry certification toward state license renewal

sections.heading: Is National Registry certification the same as a state EMS license?

blocks.text: No. National Registry certification is a national credential, while the authority to practice comes from a state EMS office license or certification. The National Registry tells clinicians to check the license renewal requirements of every state where they are licensed, because state rules can differ from, or add to, the national recertification standard.

Many states accept current National Registry certification as one way to meet their own renewal requirements. Wisconsin, for example, lets EMS clinicians meet the state continuing education requirement by holding current NREMT certification valid on the first day of the state's three year renewal period, as described on the [Wisconsin Department of Health Services renewal page](https://www.dhs.wisconsin.gov/ems/licensing/renewal.htm). That is why an employer's records need to track both credentials.

sections.heading: How often must EMS clinicians recertify with the National Registry?

blocks.text: Every two years. The National Registry's [EMT recertification page](https://www.nremt.org/EMT/Recertification) states that nationally registered EMTs "are required to renew their certification every two (2) years" and can recertify either by taking the cognitive examination or by completing continuing education. The same two year rule appears for EMRs, AEMTs and Paramedics.

Recertification cycles start when the application is approved, and the new expiration date is two years after the current expiration date on the clinician's account, so recertifying early does not shorten the next cycle. EMT, AEMT and Paramedic certifications expire on March 31. EMR certifications expire on September 30, with the examination window running from October 1 one year before expiry.

sections.heading: How many continuing education credits does each level need?

blocks.text: The NCCP divides each level's total into a national component (50%), a local or state component (25%) and an individual component (25%). The National Registry's [recertification overview](https://www.nremt.org/document/recertification) describes the national component as reflecting current evidence based medicine, scope of practice changes and position papers, with a focus on low frequency, high criticality presentations.

blocks.text: The local or state component may be defined by the state, region or agency, typically protocols, specialty areas or quality improvement findings. If none is specified, those credits are flexible but must relate directly to EMS patient care. The individual component is always flexible within that limit. The [Paramedic recertification page](https://www.nremt.org/Paramedic/Recertification) and the other level pages state these splits.

sections.heading: What changed with the 2025 NCCP model?

blocks.text: The National Registry replaced the national component topics with a 2025 NCCP model, effective April 1, 2025 for EMTs, AEMTs and Paramedics and October 1, 2025 for EMRs. Its overview states that the earlier national component requirements applied to expiration dates through September 30, 2025. As at November 2026, clinicians in a cycle that started under the new model should use the 2025 topic list, published by the National Registry, for their national credits.

blocks.title: Point to confirm
blocks.text: The topic hours inside the 2025 national component are published in a separate National Registry document that could not be read for this page. Training officers should take the national topic breakdown from that document directly rather than from secondary summaries.

sections.heading: What education does the National Registry accept?

blocks.text: The National Registry accepts education accepted by a state EMS office or accredited by the Commission on Accreditation for Pre-Hospital Continuing Education (CAPCE), education from EMS education programs, and US accredited academic credit, subject to its alternative recertification credits policy. All education must relate directly to EMS patient care, and since 2022 there is no limit on online education.

Some activities never count: duplicate courses, clinical rotations, instructor courses, management or leadership courses, performance of duty, preceptor hours, serving as a skill examiner and volunteer time with agencies. Courses with the same content or title from the same program, instructor or organization in one cycle are treated as duplicates.

sections.heading: What is needed for active status and skills verification?

blocks.text: Active status requires affiliation with an EMS agency or service and skills verified by a training officer, and for AEMTs and Paramedics also by a medical director. Clinicians not providing patient care at their level, not affiliated with an agency, or unable to get skills verified can renew as inactive, but must still complete the continuing education requirements.

AEMTs and Paramedics who recertify by examination are recertified with inactive status and must submit an inactive to active request to their medical director. Each clinician may make one examination attempt in the final year of the cycle, between April 1 and March 31 for EMTs, AEMTs and Paramedics.

sections.heading: What happens after the deadline, and how are applications audited?

blocks.text: Applications submitted after March 31 can still be accepted until April 30 with a $50 late or reinstatement fee, but all continuing education must have been completed by March 31. The National Registry states that it is required to conduct random audits of applications and that clinicians should keep all recertification supporting documentation for at least three years.

State timelines run separately. Wisconsin's late renewal process for licenses that expired on June 30, 2026, for instance, requires education completed by June 30, 2026 and the application completed by December 31, 2026. For records design, see [how to prepare training records for an audit](/guides/how-to-prepare-training-records-for-an-audit).

sections.heading: How can an EMS agency map recertification to roles and evidence?

blocks.text: An agency's training officer carries part of the obligation through skills verification, so the agency's own records matter as much as the clinician's transcript. The mapping below is an original summary for a service with mixed certification levels, suited to a [training matrix](/guides/how-to-build-a-training-matrix).

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry models the NCCP's national, local and individual components as distinct requirement sets, so a protocol update from a state EMS office lands in the local component and a National Registry model change lands in the national one. Skills verification is recorded as assessment evidence, separate from attendance. See [government and defense](/industries/government-defence) for public safety settings.

faqs.q: Can EMTs recertify with the National Registry by exam instead of continuing education?
faqs.a: Yes. EMRs, EMTs, AEMTs and Paramedics may recertify by taking the cognitive examination, with one attempt allowed in the final year of the cycle. AEMTs and Paramedics who pass are recertified as inactive and must request active status through their medical director. Those who fail can still recertify by continuing education completed by the expiration date.

faqs.q: Is there a limit on online continuing education for National Registry recertification?
faqs.a: No. The National Registry states that as of 2022 there are no limits on how much online education can be used on a recertification application. The education must still be accepted by a state EMS office or accredited by CAPCE, or come from another accepted source, and relate directly to EMS patient care.

faqs.q: Does an expired National Registry certification end a state EMS license?
faqs.a: Not automatically. State EMS offices license practice and set their own renewal rules. Some states accept current National Registry certification to meet their continuing education requirement, so letting it lapse may mean completing a state refresher course instead. Check the relevant state EMS office.

faqs.q: How long should EMS clinicians keep recertification records?
faqs.a: At least three years, according to the National Registry, which conducts random audits of recertification applications. Agencies should keep copies of skills verification records for at least the same period.
